गोरखपुर में तेज धूप और उमस से लोग परेशान:हल्की बारिश की संभावना, तापमान में गिरावट से मिलेगी राहत
- कॉपी लिंक
गोरखपुर में मंगलवार सुबह से ही आसमान पूरी तरह साफ रहा और तेज, चुभने वाली धूप निकलते ही गर्मी ने अपना असर दिखाना शुरू कर दिया। सुबह के समय से ही बाहर निकलने वाले लोगों को तेज धूप और बढ़ती गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ा। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार आज अधिकतम तापमान 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 24 डिग्री के आसपास रहने का अनुमान है।
जैसे-जैसे दिन आगे बढ़ेगा, धूप और तेज होती जाएगी, जिससे गर्मी के साथ उमस भी बढ़ेगी। खासकर दोपहर के समय हालात और मुश्किल हो सकते हैं। हवा में नमी ज्यादा होने के कारण पसीना जल्दी सूख नहीं रहा, जिससे लोगों को चिपचिपी गर्मी का एहसास हो रहा है और बाहर निकलना मुश्किल लग रहा है।
अगले 5-7 दिन मौसम रहेगा ‘ऑन-ऑफ’ मोड में
मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक गोरखपुर में आने वाले 5 से 7 दिनों तक मौसम का मिजाज लगातार बदलता रहेगा। कभी तेज धूप तो कभी बादलों की आवाजाही देखने को मिलेगी। इस दौरान बीच-बीच में हल्की बारिश या गरज-चमक के साथ बूंदाबांदी होने के भी आसार हैं, जिससे मौसम में उतार-चढ़ाव बना रहेगा।
मौसम वैज्ञानिक डॉ. कैलाश पांडेय के अनुसार शनिवार से एक बार फिर हल्की बारिश का दौर शुरू हो सकता है। बादल छाने और बारिश होने से तापमान में हल्की गिरावट दर्ज होगी, जिससे लोगों को गर्मी और उमस से कुछ राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है।
तापमान रहेगा सामान्य, लेकिन धूप में लगेगी गर्मी
अगले कुछ दिनों में दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 31 से 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच बना रहेगा, जबकि रात का न्यूनतम तापमान 23 से 24 डिग्री के आसपास रहने का अनुमान है। हालांकि तापमान ज्यादा नहीं बढ़ेगा, लेकिन तेज धूप के कारण दिन में गर्मी महसूस होती रहेगी। वहीं, बादल और बारिश के चलते बीच-बीच में मौसम सुहाना भी हो सकता है।
तेज हवाओं से बदलेगा मौसम इस दौरान हवा की रफ्तार 25 से 35 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा तक पहुंच सकती है, जिससे मौसम में तेजी से बदलाव देखने को मिलेगा। हालांकि, नमी (ह्यूमिडिटी) अधिक रहने के कारण उमस बनी रहेगी और लोगों को चिपचिपी गर्मी से लगातार जूझना पड़ेगा।
कुल मिलाकर गोरखपुर में आने वाले दिनों में मौसम पूरी तरह स्थिर नहीं रहेगा। कभी तेज धूप, कभी बादल और हल्की बारिश के बीच मौसम बदलता रहेगा। ऐसे में लोगों को एक ओर गर्मी और उमस का सामना करना पड़ेगा, तो दूसरी ओर बीच-बीच में बारिश से राहत भी मिलती रहेगी।

आज लाओ काई , होआ बिन्ह, थुक फान, वियत त्रि, होआ लू और होआन किएम जैसे वार्डों में 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान के साथ गर्म मौसम रहेगा। अन्य क्षेत्रों में आमतौर पर तापमान 33-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा।
मध्य वियतनाम के उत्तरी भाग में आज पूरे दिन धूप खिली रहेगी, दोपहर में काफी गर्मी रहेगी, तापमान 3 से 34 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा और तिन्ह गिया, डोंग हा और फु शुआन वार्डों में 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा। मध्य वियतनाम के दक्षिणी भाग में, हाई चाऊ और कैम थान वार्डों में गर्मी रहेगी, तापमान 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा। अन्य वार्डों में तापमान 32-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा। दोपहर बाद और शाम को कैम थान, तुय होआ, न्हा ट्रांग और फान थिएट वार्डों में गरज के साथ बारिश की संभावना है।
मध्य पर्वतमाला में मौसम सुहावना रहेगा, कई स्थानों पर तापमान 30-31 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक और कोन तुम में 32 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा। दोपहर बाद और शाम को छिटपुट गरज के साथ बारिश होने की संभावना है, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश और भूस्खलन का खतरा भी है।
आज सुबह से दोपहर तक दक्षिणी वियतनाम में तेज़ धूप खिली रहेगी, जिससे अधिकांश क्षेत्रों में अधिकतम तापमान 31-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा और गर्मी रहेगी। दोपहर बाद और शाम को क्षेत्र के एक तिहाई से अधिक हिस्से में छिटपुट बारिश की संभावना है, कुछ क्षेत्रों में मध्यम से भारी बारिश हो सकती है। गरज-चमक के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज़ हवाओं से सावधान रहें।
बारिश थम गई है, लेकिन ज्वार बढ़ने के कारण कई इलाकों में अभी भी भीषण बाढ़ का खतरा बना हुआ है। पूर्वानुमानों के अनुसार, आज हाऊ नदी ( कैन थो स्टेशन से होकर), तिएन नदी (माई थुआन स्टेशन से होकर) और साइगॉन नदी (फू आन और थू दाऊ मोट स्टेशनों से होकर) में जलस्तर बाढ़ चेतावनी स्तर 3 से 2-35 सेंटीमीटर अधिक रहेगा।
समुद्र में, होआंग सा विशेष क्षेत्र में हल्की बारिश, हल्की हवाएं और 10 किमी से अधिक दृश्यता देखी जा रही है। का माऊ से आन जियांग तक और ट्रूंग सा विशेष क्षेत्र के दक्षिण में स्थित समुद्री क्षेत्र में गरज के साथ तूफान जारी है, जिसमें बवंडर और तेज हवाओं का खतरा 7-8 स्तर तक पहुंच सकता है।
इस सप्ताह उत्तरी वियतनाम में दो शीत मोर्चों का सामना करना पड़ रहा है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
इस सप्ताह दो शीत मोर्चों के आने की प्रबल संभावना है, जिनमें से पहला 30 सितंबर की रात से आने का अनुमान है। विशेष रूप से, उत्तरी वियतनाम एक कमजोर, पूर्व की ओर बढ़ने वाले शीत मोर्चे से प्रभावित होगा, जिसके परिणामस्वरूप कुछ क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है।
1 और 2 अक्टूबर को तापमान में 28 सितंबर की तुलना में लगभग 2-4 डिग्री सेल्सियस की गिरावट आने की उम्मीद है।
4 अक्टूबर की रात से 5 अक्टूबर की सुबह तक ठंडी हवा का दबाव बढ़ने की संभावना है। उत्तरी क्षेत्रों में गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, कुछ इलाकों में भारी वर्षा हो सकती है और तापमान गिरकर 26-28 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा, जिससे मौसम ठंडा हो जाएगा।

इंदौर मौसम: दिन में चुभती गर्मी और रात में रिकॉर्ड तोड़ ठंड, 48 घंटे में 5.6 डिग्री लुढ़का तापमान
सार
इंदौर में मानसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम बदल गया है। बीती रात न्यूनतम तापमान 16.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज हुआ। पचमढ़ी को पीछे छोड़कर इंदौर प्रदेश में सबसे ठंडा रहा, जबकि दिन में गर्मी बनी हुई है।
विज्ञापन
विस्तार
मानसून की विदाई के इस दौर में इंदौर के मौसम ने अचानक करवट लेना शुरू कर दिया है। शहर में दिन के समय भले ही तेज गर्मी और धूप का प्रभाव बना हुआ है, लेकिन रात के तापमान में आई अचानक गिरावट ने ठंड की शुरुआत का अहसास करा दिया है। सोमवार रात इंदौर का पारा गिरकर 16.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। यह सितंबर महीने में पिछले 10 वर्षों में दर्ज किया गया सबसे कम न्यूनतम तापमान माना जा रहा है। विशेष बात यह भी रही कि यह पूरे प्रदेश में दर्ज किया गया सबसे कम तापमान था, जिससे बीती रात इंदौर मध्य प्रदेश का सबसे ठंडा शहर बन गया।
48 घंटे में 5.6 डिग्री गिरा रात का पारा
मौसम के आंकड़ों के अनुसार, केवल 48 घंटे के भीतर रात के तापमान में 5.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बड़ी गिरावट देखी गई है। बीते 27 सितंबर की रात न्यूनतम तापमान 22.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज हुआ था, जो 28 सितंबर को घटकर 19.6 डिग्री और 29 सितंबर को सीधे 16.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार यह तापमान सामान्य स्तर से भी लगभग 4 डिग्री कम दर्ज किया गया है। तापमान में आई इस अचानक गिरावट की वजह से रात के समय लोगों को तेज ठंडक महसूस हुई। मौसम में आए इस अचानक बदलाव को देखकर आम नागरिकों के साथ-साथ मौसम विशेषज्ञ भी हैरान हैं।
पचमढ़ी को पीछे छोड़कर इंदौर बना सबसे ठंडा
सामान्य तौर पर प्रदेश में सबसे कम न्यूनतम तापमान पचमढ़ी में दर्ज किया जाता है, लेकिन कल रात इंदौर पचमढ़ी से भी अधिक ठंडा दर्ज किया गया। इंदौर में जहां न्यूनतम तापमान 16.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, वहीं दूसरे स्थान पर धार दर्ज हुआ, जहां न्यूनतम तापमान 17.4 डिग्री रहा। पचमढ़ी 18 डिग्री सेल्सियस न्यूनतम तापमान के साथ तीसरे स्थान पर आ गया। इसके बाद 18.4 डिग्री के साथ छिंदवाड़ा और 18.8 डिग्री के साथ बैतूल रहा। उज्जैन में न्यूनतम तापमान 19 डिग्री और भोपाल में 19.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया।

दिन में चुभती गर्मी और रात में ठंडक
रात के न्यूनतम तापमान ने जहां ठंडक के नए रिकॉर्ड बनाए हैं, वहीं कल दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 32.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। इससे दिन और रात के तापमान के बीच एक बड़ा अंतर देखने को मिल रहा है। स्थिति यह है कि रात की तुलना में दिन का तापमान लगभग दोगुना बना हुआ है, जिससे दिन में लोगों को तीखी गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ रहा है।
सितंबर महीने में 10 साल का टूटा रिकॉर्ड
आंकड़ों के मुताबिक, सितंबर के महीने में पिछले 10 वर्षों के दौरान न्यूनतम तापमान कभी भी 17 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे नहीं गया था। बीते 10 साल में सबसे कम न्यूनतम तापमान वर्ष 2018 में 18.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया था। इसके बाद वर्ष 2024 में न्यूनतम तापमान 20.1 डिग्री और वर्ष 2025 में 20.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा था। इस बार 16.6 डिग्री तापमान दर्ज होने से पिछले एक दशक के सभी रिकॉर्ड टूट गए हैं। हालांकि, इंदौर के मौसम इतिहास में सितंबर माह का सबसे कम तापमान 2 सितंबर 2000 को दर्ज किया गया था, जब न्यूनतम पारा गिरकर 9 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया था।

राजस्थान में बारिश का आखिरी दौर: आज तीन संभागों में मेघगर्जन के साथ बौछारें, तेज हवाओं के बाद बढ़ेगी गर्मी
राजस्थान में 29 सितंबर को कुछ इलाकों में बारिश और तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं। इसके बाद बारिश घटेगी और अगले दिनों में तापमान बढ़ने के आसार हैं।
विस्तार
राजस्थान में मानसून की विदाई के साथ बारिश का दायरा लगातार सिमट रहा है। हालांकि पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के असर से मंगलवार, 29 सितंबर को जयपुर, अजमेर और भरतपुर संभागों में कहीं-कहीं मेघगर्जन के साथ बारिश हो सकती है। बीकानेर संभाग में भी कुछ स्थानों पर हल्की बारिश के आसार हैं। इस दौरान 40 से 50 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं।
इसके बाद प्रदेश में बारिश की गतिविधियां कमजोर पड़ने लगेंगी। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार 29 सितंबर के बाद पश्चिमी राजस्थान और 30 सितंबर से पूर्वी राजस्थान में बारिश का दौर काफी कम होने की संभावना है। पश्चिमी राजस्थान में 29 सितंबर के बाद कोई चेतावनी नहीं है, जबकि पूर्वी राजस्थान में भी 30 सितंबर से अगले दिनों के लिए कोई मौसम चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है।
मानसून की विदाई के साथ बदलने लगेगा मौसम
राजस्थान से मानसून की वापसी आगे बढ़ रही है। मानसून की विदाई के साथ वातावरण में नमी कम होगी और बारिश के दौर में लगातार कमी आएगी। ऐसे में अगले कुछ दिनों में धूप का असर बढ़ने और दिन के तापमान में बढ़ोतरी होने की संभावना है।
हालांकि सुबह और रात के समय कई इलाकों में हल्की ठंडक महसूस हो सकती है। मौसम में यह बदलाव मानसून की विदाई के साथ सामान्य रूप से देखने को मिलता है।
यह भी पढें- राजस्थान: बच्चे के पासपोर्ट पर पिता का नाम जरूरी नहीं, हाईकोर्ट ने सुनाया अहम फैसला
पश्चिमी राजस्थान में फिर बढ़ेगी गर्मी
बारिश का असर कम होने के बाद पश्चिमी राजस्थान में तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना है। सोमवार को फलोदी में प्रदेश का सबसे अधिक 39.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया गया था। आने वाले दिनों में पश्चिमी जिलों में धूप और शुष्क मौसम के कारण पारा फिर ऊपर जा सकता है।
जयपुर-अजमेर-भरतपुर में आज आखिरी सक्रियता के आसार
मंगलवार को जयपुर, अजमेर और भरतपुर संभागों में स्थानीय स्तर पर बादल बनने और गरज-चमक के साथ बौछारें पड़ने की संभावना है। कुछ स्थानों पर तेज हवाओं का असर भी देखने को मिल सकता है। बीकानेर संभाग में भी हल्की बारिश हो सकती है।इसके बाद मौसम मुख्यतः शुष्क रहने का अनुमान है। यानी राजस्थान में आज बारिश और तेज हवाओं का असर, इसके बाद मौसम साफ और तापमान में बढ़ोतरी का दौर देखने को मिल सकता है।
आगे कैसा रहेगा मौसम?
- 29 सितंबर: जयपुर, अजमेर, भरतपुर और कुछ अन्य इलाकों में गरज-चमक के साथ बारिश की संभावना।

- पश्चिमी राजस्थान: मौसम मुख्यतः शुष्क रहेगा और तापमान बढ़ सकता है।

How public schools can protect children from extreme heat
A recent study indicates that if global temperatures rise by 1.5 degrees Celsius, 2.5 crore children in Bangladesh could experience five or more months of heat stress. If global temperatures rise by 2 degrees Celsius, the number is projected to be even higher. This risk is particularly significant for children in urban areas, where rising temperatures are compounded by the heat island effect.
This year’s extended monsoon, combined with rising temperatures, has made heat increasingly difficult for us. On September 27, the country’s highest temperature—35.5 degrees Celsius—was recorded in Dhaka, Khulna, and Chandpur. As the temperature was close to heatwave levels, the heat felt intense. For young children, the consequences are severe and extend beyond physical discomfort. Prolonged exposure to heat can affect their health, cognitive ability, and learning.
The human body regulates its temperature through sweating, known as thermoregulation. In high temperatures, sweat carries heat from the body and removes it as it evaporates. But evaporation becomes difficult when the surrounding air contains high levels of moisture. In our tropical monsoon climate, high humidity makes it difficult for the body to cool itself naturally. When high humidity is combined with rising temperatures, the “feels like” temperature increases and the body is pushed closer to its thermal limits.
For young children, these conditions pose greater risks. Immature thermoregulation makes them sweat less and overheat more quickly, making them more vulnerable to heat stress. Studies have linked heat stress among children with heat-related illness, hospital visits, asthma exacerbation, and worsening digestive and renal conditions.
The effects of heat are not limited to children’s physical health. Excessive heat also affects their concentration and cognitive ability. Teachers have reported fatigue, distraction, reduced attention, and irritation among students. With prolonged exposure, these effects can translate into loss of learning. Longitudinal studies have found that a 1-degree Fahrenheit increase in temperature reduces academic performance by 1 percent.
The growing body of evidence underscores the need to address the adverse effects of increasingly frequent heatwaves on children. However, at a national scale, ensuring protection from heat at home for every child is difficult, particularly where families’ socioeconomic conditions limit access to resilient homes, cooling technologies, and other adaptive measures. This creates an opportunity to protect our children where they are brought together at scale: in public schools.
Children spend a substantial part of their waking hours at school each day, making classroom conditions an important part of their daily exposure to heat. Public schools, in particular, serve large numbers of children, including those who have limited protection from heat at home. They can therefore provide a more equitable point of intervention. Yet many public schools lack adequate measures to provide comfortable thermal conditions. Improving these conditions should be treated as part of protecting children’s health and learning.
The first step is to reduce heat gain within school buildings. The amount of heat entering a classroom depends on decisions made long before children occupy it, including the design of roofs and walls. Reflective roofs and walls with appropriate insulation can reduce heat entering through the building envelope. New public-school construction should incorporate these climate-responsive design requirements, while older schools should have retrofit guidelines to make necessary changes.
But reducing heat gain is only part of the challenge. Humidity is an inherent part of our geographical climate, and our buildings must be designed around it. This principle was reflected in a recent conversation I had with prominent architect Rafiq Azam, who designed the Aga Khan Academy based on features of our tropical monsoon climate. He emphasised the need for school architecture to align with our climatic features through a combination of passive and active techniques.
Passive solutions include shading and natural ventilation. Shading by trees and green roofs can reduce direct exposure and lower indoor temperatures, while cross-ventilation, supported by additional fans, can improve air movement. Together, these measures can make indoor conditions more tolerable in humid heat.
Where passive measures are insufficient, and resources permit, air conditioning should also be considered. Research has found that classroom air conditioning can mitigate the negative effects of high temperatures on learning outcomes. It may not be feasible for every school, but targeted investment could provide controlled environments during the hottest periods. Such investment could prioritise schools serving children who are particularly vulnerable to heat because of poor housing conditions.
These measures should not be treated as a separate climate agenda. They should be integrated into existing investments in school infrastructure, safety and learning environments. The current approach to protecting children from heat remains largely reactive, with school closures when temperatures reach dangerous levels. While closures can protect children during extreme heat, they do not address students’ experience on days when temperatures remain close to thresholds, nor do they protect children from heat in their homes. As extreme heat becomes a recurring feature of our climate, protecting children requires a more systematic approach.
Climate-responsive schools could also serve a wider public purpose. As extreme heat becomes an increasingly important urban climate risk, appropriately designed and safely managed school spaces could function as community cooling centres during dangerous heat events. Bangladesh already has a precedent for using schools as cyclone shelters and relief centres. The same public infrastructure could be adapted to provide refuge during extreme heat events, which are common these days.
Significant investments are already underway to improve school infrastructure. Thermal comfort should be treated as an integral component of such investments. Alongside infrastructure, heat-safety measures should also be incorporated into broader school-safety initiatives under the government’s School Level Improvement Plan (SLIP). As SLIP provides resources for school-level improvements, these investments should also address thermal conditions, making school environments resilient to a changing climate.
We may not be moving fast enough to stop the world from getting hotter, but we can still determine how much heat affects our children’s health, learning and development. We have an opportunity to better equip our public schools to protect children from the adverse effects of an extreme climate. As the government seeks to reform the education system, heat considerations should be mainstreamed into education policies and practices. Investing in heat-resilient schools is an investment in healthier children, better learning, and a more climate-ready future.
Maisha Bint Salam is sustainability expert at Nexus360, currently pursuing her master’s at the University of Cambridge in the UK.

by Mareeam Tomomi Ahmed in World on 29th September, 2026
Summer ‘26 wasn’t like the other summers. From wildfires to droughts, floods to extreme heat, all nations have experienced new climate catastrophes and found new responsibilities we’ve had to bear. In the UK, we might be breathing a sigh of relief as a difficult summer comes to an end, and we may not have to worry about intense heat for a while. But the dry summer, paired with a lack of water reserves and failed crops, means that we are officially running out of water and affordable food in the UK.
Often, conversations about food are cloaked in language like “production” and “systems,” which suggests that technological and industrial forces are the only ones at play when it comes to getting the food on our shelves. What this masks, however, is that, at the most basic level, we depend wholly on the natural world for survival.
Collectively, we must internalise that food does not magically appear in the supermarket shrink-wrapped in plastic. It comes from fields and greenhouses, farms and paddies, animals and plants.
Stable food growing requires predictable weather patterns and for farmers and growers to be prepared as the seasons change, but the climate catastrophe is making this increasingly impossible.
Currently, in 2026, we sit at 1.56°C (±0.09) higher than pre-industrial temperatures, with the highest month being this July. This might not sound significant, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has created a threshold of 1.5°C, where anything higher is disastrous for human life and ecosystems. In fact, the UN warns that it is already too late.
The Executive Director of the UN Environmental Programme, Inger Andersen, emphasises that
“there are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C. Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer.”
This is devastating – but unsurprising, as many of us have already been living through extreme temperatures. Be it the 220 hectares of wildfire in Wales or London boroughs like Havering or Walthamstow, which saw huge fires too. For the first time, we’ve seen:
For many in the UK, extreme heat and drought have forced us to recognise a climate crisis that the rest of the world has been experiencing the worst of for decades. The Yale School of the Environment diagnosed the UK with an awareness gap in the climate crisis. We’ve fallen into a perceived proximity bias to the threat of the climate crisis.
None of the landslides in Indonesia that wiped out an endangered species; fires that destroy Maui towns; the melting Himalayas and frequent glacial collapse; chronic smog in Pakistan; and droughts in Somalia mattered until it was experienced in the Western world.
Suddenly, the climate crisis is real, and it has been cemented that we will, in fact, suffer the symptoms of an atmosphere with a greater concentration of carbon. Soberingly, this is just the beginning of the frequency of climate catastrophes as predicted in the 2015 Projections of future floods and hydrological droughts in Europe under a +2°C global warming.
The El Niño weather phenomenon (where seawater warms up due to strong winds in the tropical Pacific) is “adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming” – according to Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus. Warmer seas mean stronger hurricanes and tsunamis, stronger heatwaves, shrinking ice caps, higher sea levels and greater risk of flooding.
Just this year, we’ve seen flash flooding in Nepal-Tibet at the end of August, with regular flooding episodes in Pakistan, Bangladesh and China that are deadly, killing crops and people in the immediate aftermath. Whilst flooding, hurricanes and tsunamis have long been a regular occurrence in Asia and the Americas, heatwaves and droughts are now the new norm for countries like Britain too.
This heatwave exposed how underprepared the UK’s food and water systems are – despite farmers raising concerns about the drop in yields. This year, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) announced that the UK’s arable harvest is 1.35 million tonnes lower than predicted in March 2026. Chris Jaccarini, food economist at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU), comments that
“food production is on the front line of climate change”, as farmers were not expecting such a severe drought and poor harvest.
These are factors which cause the spike in the cost of food, and Jaccarini warns that it will only get steeper as greenhouse gases become more concentrated. Tom Lancaster, Analyst of Land, Food and Farming for AHDB, emphasises that this is not an anomaly, this is the third awful harvest in a row.
Farms and growers have been raising the alarm to the government for decades about the drop in yields due to climate change, yet they were given no subsidies and funding. Now, the crisis is realised and manifested. The Food Foundation issued a press release on the 19th of August pointing the finger at the government and their lack of investment in the horticultural sector. Consequently,
the UK is heavily dependent on imports for food when 50% of the UK’s most purchased fruits and 95% of veggies can be grown domestically.
Currently, however, we import 80% of our fruit and 47% of our vegetables.
Of the top 20 countries that the UK imports the most fruit and vegetables from, 90% are moderately to severely vulnerable to climate change. 40% of Britain’s overall food is imported, and if 90% of these countries are suffering, then it is definitely our problem.
Food Policy expert Tim Lang warns of our food chain’s vulnerability to shock. The threats of shock are numerous, and Lang explores them in his National Preparedness Commission report here. As the cost of growing food, watering and exporting increases due to an uninhabitable climate, our import costs will rise, and the volume of produce imported will fall. Experts like Lang and Costelloe highlight that we are also relying on the fact that neighbouring countries may still want to share their produce. We may find ourselves stranded due to the cost and infrequency of possible harvesting. Countries may not be able to afford to feed abroad, and focus their harvests domestically.
An insecurity that results from the regular droughts is that the cost of safe water for farming and growing will increase. Aquifers will not capture enough water, triggering the construction of major water supply reservoirs across Europe. Farmers in the UK as well as Italy, Hungary and France have lost a significant volume of their harvest this year due to the long, unpredicted droughts. James Pullen, a potato grower in Somerset, was facing £200,000 losses due to his produce appearing bruised or not growing at all.
In many continents, key rivers have dried up, raising alarm bells between farmers and non-farmers.
Hungary is now facing an unprecedented energy crisis that has forced the country to shut down all but one of its Danube-cooled nuclear reactors for the first time in 44 years.
With droughts prevalent for key exporters, already struggling farmers will have to hike up costs to make ends meet for the losses. Some fruit and vegetables require a lot more water, like cauliflower, tomatoes, cucumber, strawberries, and peaches. If there is less moisture in the soil due to droughts, root vegetables like parsnips, carrots and potatoes will also struggle to grow. If there are constant water shortages, we can expect to see fewer fruit and vegetables on shelves or pay more for the ones available.
Due to a lack of grass and fodder for British cows and chickens, and the scorching temperatures, the livestock which we depend on for meat, milk, cheese, butter and eggs have whittled away. It is becoming difficult to maintain the milk and egg production necessary for the nation – a reason why eggs have soared in price since the shortage began in 2022. Unfortunately, the solution of importing eggs and poultry from Brazil brought even more health risks to British consumers, with a salmonella outbreak from the imports in August 2026.
Dairy cows typically start to suffer from heat stress when temperatures are higher than 25°C, and this year, temperatures went up to 38°C!
Farmers have reported milk yields down by 10%-15% due to this. This is the biggest decline in 5 years for the UK.
Droughts can cause a fall in production and livestock, but it can also exacerbate the spread of disease. Higher temperatures from El Niño create the conditions for the spread of airborne disease from other regions. This season, farmers have had to keep an eye out for Bluetongue in cattle and sheep which are coming from tropical regions to temperate regions. Bluetongue-carrying biting midges are likely to survive in the animals due to the UK’s distinct seasons. The longer summers and warm autumns create the ideal environment for midges to live longer and incubate faster.
If we can’t keep our livestock alive and well in these temperatures, there is little hope in the future for reliably safe and affordable staples. As well as losing reliable, fresh produce, we are at risk of losing basic necessities like eggs and milk.
This year alone, we’ve had five heatwave episodes, worsening the state of our already fragile food system. Farmers and experts warn us of a future with a loss of staple produce like tomatoes, potatoes, strawberries and carrots. If this year’s harvests have been failing, it means preparation for next year’s growing season is at a huge risk because harvests are important for seed saving to ensure a better yield for the coming growing year.
Harvests are also important for stockpiling for the winter feed, both for animals and humans. Historically, people would store the summer’s harvests in the form of pickles, fermentation and drying out. All cultures across the globe have a method of storing the harvest from summer. Over time, as harvests continue to be weak or become unsalvageable, we will lose crucial foodstuffs. Tinned tomatoes, pickles, canned fruit, kimchi, curry, miso, and soybean pastes will become dearer. On average, it’ll be the global majority communities once again who bear the brunt of the climate crisis.
Without a doubt, it is the government’s responsibility to support the nation with food affordability and provision. However, we see grassroots projects, places of worship, even supermarkets doing more for people getting food than the government. Cafes and supermarkets give their excess produce and raise money for already strained food banks.
The Right to Grow is a political campaign that is asking councils for the right to grow food on public land. It started in Hull in 2023 and is gaining traction in London. The city is one of the hottest places, with fewer people able to get outside and grow food due to work commitments and a lack of private gardens. If we were to have the right to grow in all major cities, towns and villages, more people would have access to free or affordable food and meals. It would be a significant asset to all communities and biodiversity in the face of the climate crisis and food crisis. Pam Warhurst founded Incredible Edible, which made room for the Right to Grow campaign to begin. Her vision is that,
“if you harness a different approach to investment in people and land, you get better outcomes for people and the planet.”
If more communities had accessibility to places where food can be grown and prepared, we would be able to create our own localised food system. The aim is to have small, manageable gardens where yields are high in as many neighbourhoods as possible. The average working-class household doesn’t have time to tend to fields and find organic alternatives to staple foods as the crisis deepens. In fact, they may have to work longer hours to afford a life in the climate crisis, with a higher cost of energy to cook and heat their home.
In this case, local gardens can become the place for affordable, healthy produce, if not completely free, with seasonal seed swaps and sowing sessions to teach vital life skills.
It may be that due to the cost of cooking ‘western’ staples like potatoes and chard, cultural foods like gourds, lady fingers, aubergines and chillies aren’t prioritised. Setting up skill-sharing workshops with our elders will give the chance for people to learn how to nurture cultural plants and to store harvests in jars, by pickling, fermenting or drying.
Sharing harvests, seeds and recipes in these spaces could prevent the loss of key cultural foods.
Localising community gardens with funding and shelter to come together after work, or drop by and take from, resolves only some of the stress the food system is facing. We would have to resist to maintain and keep our community growing spaces to help people survive through a climate crisis. Furthermore, making food growing a core curriculum for schools to ensure future generations can access organic and fresh food is a radical, but necessary step.
We won’t resolve the crisis independently, nor can we force big corporations and governments to restrict their carbon emissions and stop the deforestation of native trees which make way for data centres and palm oil production.
The fact of the matter is that the average household is not responsible for the sharp spike in global temperatures and loss of biodiversity, but community resilience and mobilisation is crucial in a time like this.
Communities of all backgrounds and generations must be able to grow their own food, become self-resilient and autonomous with a localised food economy, rather than fall prey to the rising costs of living. This may not create 100% self-sufficiency for the UK; however, it gives locals, working-class families and those dependent on food banks a chance to access fresh, organic foods in a climate where basic necessities are getting harder to find on supermarket shelves.
In a climate of conflict, crisis and cost of living, I hope that people power is the answer for survival and that we exercise our privilege and reach out a hand of support to those who will bear the brunt of the climate crisis.
Allah ﷻ tells us that, “whoever saves a life, it is as if they saved all of humanity.” (Surah Al-Ma’idah, 5:32)
Supporting local food-growing communities is important, as they are some of the rare places where people are supported, fed and cared for, with little cost for the consumer.
Mareeam, 27 from London is a facilitator that aims on getting people outdoors to appreciate nature and community. After being trained in research and tackling colonial thought and history she has shifted to create micro change in the immediate sense by facilitating workshops and third spaces for all minorities to engage in physically. Her interests and aspiration is to create a network of people until the resistance is firm.

A self-proclaimed ‘loo enthusiast’ has named Britain’s most luxurious toilets after inventing a rating app.
Yolanda Cuevas-Beck, 48, says she has spent her whole life judging toilets and sharing the findings with family and friends.
Now, using AI, she has managed to create her own website and app called Porcelain Report to connect a network of loo reviewers and flush out the best ones.
The finance worker from Guildford, Surrey, says the bathrooms are rated on their cleanliness, accessibility, glamour, and how well the appliances work.
A final score out of five stars is then worked out from these ratings, and it is placed onto the venue map.
Her favourite toilets are at the Ivy as they are very colourful and usually well looked after, while her least favourite is the Burger King by Waterloo Station
Yolanda said: “Sometimes you go to a restaurant which is beautiful and has lovely food but when you go to the loo it is just a box.
“I care about all the public loos. I think it is important for the establishments to know that people are looking at them.
“People are rating the food, so why can’t we also rate the loos.
“It is an essential part. If they care about what they are offering me they will have pride and make sure that they have a nice communal loo.”
Yolanda, who is originally from the Dominican Republic, says it took her about a month to set up Porcelain Report around her day job.
Her users are still slowly building, but she says that she has many passionate people writing reviews and filling out extra information such as whether the toilet is free or paid.
The site has particularly been a hit with people who require an accessible toilet, so that they can rank how well it did.
Yolanda added: “Lots of people say it is very niche and ask how I came up with this idea. But a lot of people say it is necessary to catalogue all the different loos.
“I think it is important. Once I get a lot of ratings the establishments will know what people think about their loos.
“When I started my goal was to find beautiful and clean loos, but I noticed lots of people are looking for accessible loos.
“People write paragraphs about how unhappy they are with the loos.”
She has since created a top ten list, which is constantly changing, of her favourite loos.
At the number two spot is the Sea Containers Hotel on the South Bank in Central London.
Yolanda is also very proud of her toilets at home, which she keeps spotless.
She said: “My loos at home are not only shiny but beautiful.”

Estate agency Boydens has reported selling 16 beach huts in Essex so far this year, with demand accelerating during the summer heatwave period.
The sales have been concentrated in coastal locations including Frinton-on-Sea and Walton-on-the-Naze, with hotspots at High Wall, Low Wall, The Leas, and Southcliff.
Zenna Everett, sales and lettings negotiator at Boydens’ Frinton-on-Sea office, said some properties received accepted offers within hours of coming to market. “The level of interest in acquiring beach huts has gone through the roof this summer,” she noted.
Pricing and buyer profile
Asking prices across the region range from approximately £10,000 to £60,000, depending on location. Buyers are also liable for annual licence fees payable to the relevant local authority.
The agency reported that most purchases have been made by families from inland Essex towns including Brentwood, Chelmsford, and Romford, seeking coastal access for children and grandchildren.
Five transactions completed in August, with additional sales progressing in September, indicating sustained demand beyond the peak summer period. This trend contrasts with broader market challenges affecting property transactions in other segments.
Market dynamics
The beach hut market represents a niche alternative asset class, with properties serving as recreational spaces rather than residential accommodation. Unlike traditional property investments facing headwinds in some markets, including declining flat values in certain London areas, beach huts offer lower entry points and different use cases.
Everett attributed the sales activity to the extended period of warm weather and buyers’ desire for dedicated coastal facilities. “People like the convenience of a beach hut as it gives them a base, somewhere to relax and to store their things,” she said.
The transactions indicate continued appetite for leisure property assets in accessible coastal locations within commuting distance of major population centres in southeast England.

Pune rainfall crossed the double-digit mark at Shivajinagar for the first time in 58 days on Monday evening, with the city recording sharply uneven showers and the India Meteorological Department forecasting similar conditions over the next three days.
The Shivajinagar weather station recorded 17.1 mm of rain on Monday evening. The previous double-digit reading was recorded on August 1, when the station received 30.3 mm over 24 hours. The reading dropped to 1.5 mm the following day.
The current dry spell was the second-longest period of single-digit rainfall at Shivajinagar since 2014. The longest such stretch occurred in 2018, when the weather station went 64 consecutive days without recording double-digit rain, according to an expert from the weather organisation Vagaries of the Weather.
The rain was unevenly distributed across Pune. The National Defence Academy recorded 15 mm, while Pashan received 2 mm and Hadapsar recorded 1 mm. Chinchwad, Lavale, Magarpatta and Koregaon Park did not receive rain, while Lohegaon recorded only traces.
The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds and light to moderate rain in Pune and the Pune Ghats over the next three days. A yellow alert has been issued for September 29. The forecast indicates that any further showers could remain localised rather than affecting the city uniformly.
Dr Anupam Kashyapi, former head of weather forecasting at the IMD, said the showers were indicative of the approaching withdrawal of the southwest monsoon. He said the monsoon was likely to withdraw from Mumbai and Pune by early October and from the rest of Maharashtra by the middle of October.
The rainfall comes as Maharashtra faces a 19 per cent deficit in cumulative rainfall as of September 28, even though the state has declared drought in 75 per cent of its area. The country’s cumulative rainfall deficit stands at 12 per cent, while Pune district continues to record a 14 per cent surplus for the season, according to the IMD.
Monday evening’s rain did not significantly alter temperatures in the city. Shivajinagar recorded a maximum of 33.4 degrees Celsius, while Pashan, Lohegaon, Chinchwad and Koregaon Park remained at nearly similar levels. Minimum temperatures ranged from 18.4 degrees Celsius in Pashan to 22.5 degrees Celsius in Koregaon Park.
The weather office said maximum and minimum temperatures in different parts of Pune were likely to remain broadly unchanged over the next few days.
